subject: Polity
topic: Fundamental Rights II — Arts 19-22, freedoms, detention, right against exploitation
description: Fundamental Rights: Article 19 six freedoms, reasonable restrictions, Art 20 (conviction), Art 21 (life/liberty, Maneka Gandhi), Art 22 (preventive detention), Art 23-24 (exploitation).

questions.stem: Article 19 of the Indian Constitution guarantees six fundamental freedoms. Which of the following is NOT one of them?

options.option_text: Freedom to vote in elections — electoral rights are statutory rights, not a Part III Fundamental Right
Freedom of speech and expression — this is Article 19(1)(a) (not this) instead however
Freedom to reside and settle in any part of India — this is Article 19(1)(e) (not this)
Freedom to practise any profession or occupation — this is Article 19(1)(g) (not this)

questions.explanation: ART 19 SIX FREEDOMS (originally 7; right to property removed by 44th Amendment 1978): (a) Speech and expression. (b) Peaceful assembly without arms. (c) Association or union. (d) Free movement throughout India. (e) Residence and settlement anywhere in India. (g) Practise any profession, trade, or business. NOTE: (f) was right to property — removed 1978. RIGHT TO VOTE: not Art 19; derived from Article 326 (universal adult franchise) — a constitutional right but not a Fundamental Right under Part III. PYQ: which freedom is NOT in Art 19 — SSC CGL, IBPS PO polity 1-2x per cycle.

questions.stem: Article 21 of the Indian Constitution protects the right to life and personal liberty. Through judicial interpretation, this article has been expanded to include:

options.option_text: A vast range of rights including right to health, right to privacy, right to livelihood, right to education
Only physical survival; it does not extend to quality of life or dignity under any interpretation
The right to vote, right to property, and right to social security under Art 21 alone
Exclusively procedural protections during criminal arrest; not broader life aspects at all

questions.explanation: ART 21: 'No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.' MANEKA GANDHI CASE (1978): procedure must be FAIR, JUST, REASONABLE (overruled A.K. Gopalan 1950). EXPANDED RIGHTS UNDER ART 21: right to livelihood, right to privacy (Puttaswamy 2017 — 9-judge bench), right to health, right to speedy trial, right to legal aid, right to die with dignity (passive euthanasia — Aruna Shanbaug 2011), right to education (before Art 21A was inserted by 86th Amendment 2002). ART 21 is the MOST EXPANSIVE fundamental right. PYQ: Art 21 expansion in UPSC, IBPS PO 1-2x per year.

questions.stem: Under Article 22, a person arrested without a warrant must be produced before a magistrate within:

options.option_text: 24 hours of arrest — excluding travel time from place of arrest to court
48 hours — Art 22 specifically provides the 24-hour maximum, not 48 hours
72 hours — a three-day limit exists in some other legal systems but not under Art 22
Within the same calendar day regardless of distance or travel time involved

questions.explanation: ART 22(2): Every arrested person must be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 HOURS of arrest (excluding journey time). RIGHTS UNDER ART 22: (1) Right to be informed of grounds of arrest. (2) Right to consult and be defended by a lawyer. (3) 24-hour magistrate production. EXCEPTIONS: Art 22(3) — these protections do NOT apply to enemy aliens or persons arrested under preventive detention law. PREVENTIVE DETENTION: advisory board must review detention beyond 3 months. LANDMARK: Joginder Kumar Case (1994); D.K. Basu Case (1997) — detailed arrest/detention guidelines. PYQ: 24-hour rule under Art 22 in IBPS PO, SSC polity.

questions.stem: Article 23 of the Indian Constitution prohibits traffic in human beings. Under this article, the Parliament has enacted which law for enforcement?

options.option_text: Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956 — specifically enacted under Art 23 to combat human trafficking
Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 — this was enacted under Art 24, not Art 23
Prevention of Atrocities Act, 1989 — this addresses caste discrimination, not trafficking specifically
POCSO Act, 2012 — this protects children from sexual offences broadly, not limited to Art 23

questions.explanation: ART 23: prohibits traffic in human beings and forced labour (begar). ART 24: prohibits employment of children below 14 in hazardous work. ENFORCEMENT LEGISLATION: Art 23 → Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act 1956 (ITPA). Art 24 → Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986, amended 2016. BONDED LABOUR: Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1976 also under Art 23. EXCEPTION: Art 23(2) — State may impose compulsory service for public purposes (NCC, NSS). PYQ: Art 23 enforcement act in IBPS PO, SSC polity.

questions.stem: The freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) can be restricted by Parliament on which of the following grounds?

options.option_text: Sovereignty/integrity of India, state security, public order, friendly foreign relations, decency, contempt of court, defamation, incitement to offence
Only national security grounds — speech restrictions are limited to defence-related matters alone (not this) instead however
The President alone can restrict speech without Parliamentary legislation on these grounds (not this) instead however
Any ground the State deems necessary — Art 19(2) imposes no enumerated limits on restriction (not this) instead however

questions.explanation: ART 19(2): Eight grounds for restricting free speech (added by First Amendment, 1951): (1) Sovereignty and integrity of India. (2) Security of the State. (3) Friendly relations with foreign States. (4) Public order. (5) Decency or morality. (6) Contempt of court. (7) Defamation. (8) Incitement to an offence. REASONABLENESS TEST: restrictions must be reasonable and not excessive. INTERNET SHUTDOWN: SC held internet access is a right under Art 19(1)(a); shutdown must follow Art 19(2) grounds. PYQ: Art 19(2) grounds in UPSC, IBPS PO polity 1-2x per cycle.

questions.stem: Article 20(2) of the Indian Constitution embodies which principle of criminal law?

options.option_text: Double jeopardy — no person shall be prosecuted or punished for the same offence more than once
Presumption of innocence — a common law principle; not explicitly stated in Art 20
Right to speedy trial — this has been read into Art 21, not codified in Art 20
Retrospective punishment — Art 20(1) prohibits this; Art 20(2) is a separate distinct provision

questions.explanation: ART 20 — THREE PROTECTIONS: (1) Art 20(1): Ex post facto laws prohibited — no punishment for act that was not an offence when committed. (2) Art 20(2): DOUBLE JEOPARDY — 'nemo debet bis vexari' (no one tried twice for same offence). (3) Art 20(3): Self-incrimination protection — no person accused of offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself. NOTE: Art 20 CANNOT be suspended even during national emergency (unlike Arts 19 and 21 before the 44th Amendment). PYQ: Art 20 sub-clauses + double jeopardy in UPSC Prelims, IBPS PO polity.

questions.stem: In the Maneka Gandhi case (1978), the Supreme Court overruled its earlier A.K. Gopalan (1950) interpretation of Article 21 by holding that:

options.option_text: The procedure for depriving liberty must be fair, just, and reasonable — not merely any procedure authorised by law
Art 21 and Art 19 operate independently; the validity of a law under one is irrelevant to the other
Personal liberty includes only physical freedom from bodily restraint, not broader rights
Parliament may pass any detention procedure without judicial review of its fairness or reasonableness

questions.explanation: A.K. GOPALAN (1950): SC held Arts 19, 21, 22 operate in separate watertight compartments; any 'procedure established by law' (even unfair) suffices for Art 21. MANEKA GANDHI (1978): SC overruled Gopalan. Held: (1) Arts 14, 19, 21 must all be satisfied simultaneously — they are not mutually exclusive. (2) 'Procedure established by law' must be RIGHT, JUST, FAIR — due process embedded into Art 21. (3) Right to travel abroad is part of Art 21. IMPACT: enormous expansion of Art 21; all socio-economic rights read into Art 21 became possible after this judgment. PYQ: Maneka Gandhi case in UPSC Prelims 1-2x per year — top 5 most cited SC cases.
